summary: Distinguish background batch vs interactive token accounting — guidance for quota and burst pool config
description: Issue summary: Customer reports repeated 429s during nightly background embedding backfills while interactive chat traffic is concurrently hitting the same tenant. Impact: Background pipeline (bulk embedding) experiences sustained throttling, causing missed SLA for nightly jobs; interactive chat users intermittently see latency spikes and 429s. Environment: Dedicated pool (customer-reserved), prod, us-east primary. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start the nightly backfill job (60 concurrent workers sending embedding->create calls). 2) Simultaneously open 50 interactive chat sessions in the UI. 3) Observe token throttle headers and 429 responses after ~10–15 minutes. Observed behavior: 429s surface for both background and interactive routes; token headers show "X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0" and burst credits depleted. Console shows a single tenant-level token bucket being used for both route types. Expected behavior: Ability to isolate background batch accounting from interactive low-latency traffic via route-level quotas or separate burst pools so background jobs can be rate-limited without impacting interactive sessions. Customer asks: 1) How to configure route-level separation and burst pools for a dedicated tenant. 2) Whether we can create a policy that deprioritizes background jobs automatically without manual orchestration. 3) Recommendations for smoothing and refill windows for mixed workloads.

investigation_notes: Logs and traces: sample request ids: req-8a2f, req-8a34, req-8b11. We pulled rate-limiter metrics for tenant T-99321 between 2026-03-10T02:00Z and 2026-03-10T04:00Z: refill_rate ~ 120 tokens/min, burst_window configured at default 30s. Observed pattern: background workers created synchronized request waves every minute (cron-aligned), causing token surge; autoscaler warmup probes (health-checks) also contributed ~700 token/min transient. Hypothesis: tenant-level token bucket combined with default burst_window collapses both interactive and background traffic into the same accounting domain — result is contention where background bursts deplete burst credits that interactive sessions expect to use for low-latency bursts. We also saw evidence of ephemeral API keys used by the background workers which increased fanout (multiple keys sharing same tenant bucket), amplifying counting complexities. Temporary reproducer: reducing concurrency to 20 eliminated interactive 429s in our test cluster. Metrics links: https://console.redwood.com/tenants/T-99321/rate-limiter-metrics, dashboard: RateLimiter - tenant T-99321
resolution: Short-term workaround applied: advised customer to 1) Stagger backfill start time across workers (randomized jitter of 0–300s) and lower concurrency to 20; 2) Use a single long-lived API key for the backfill process instead of creating many ephemeral keys; 3) Configure background jobs to use a lower-priority route tag (background) and interactive clients to use high-priority tag (interactive). These steps were implemented by the customer on 2026-03-11 and reduced 429s within one run. Medium-term fix: We recommended creating a dedicated burst pool for background routes on the customer's dedicated pool. Action items (owner): - Marco Ruiz: open INT change to enable per-route burst_pool allocation for T-99321 (INT-423) — done. - Platform: add route-level smoothing policy option to console (tracked in github PR https://github.com/redwood/infra/pull/5312). Long-term: Add a runbook for hybrid workload customers describing quota separation patterns, route tagging, and autoscaler warmup tuning. Follow-ups: schedule a 1:1 configuration review with Streamline Analytics next week; create console guidance that surfaces route-level quota usage and recommended defaults for mixed workloads.
